previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of CAD, CABG, COPD, CVA, and hypothyroidism was admitted for left leg swelling and chest pain. Workup revealed no pulmonary embolism or acute cardiac ischemia. Abdominal pain was attributed to urinary retention with a markedly distended bladder, which improved after Foley catheter placement. He developed transient atrial fibrillation with RVR, managed with rate control, but medication was stopped due to bradycardia. A new cough and chest X-ray changes led to treatment for mild bacterial pneumonia. He failed two voiding trials, so was discharged home with a catheter and tamsulosin. Chronic issues like diverticulosis, SMA stenosis, and an incidental L4 vertebral finding were noted for outpatient follow-up. He stabilized, tolerated a regular diet, and was discharged in stable condition with home health services.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ yo M, with a history of CAD s/p distant 
CABG, CVA, on plavix, EtOH abuse, presented with 3 days of 
nausea, vomiting, and RUQ pain, and was found to have alcoholic 
hepatitis.

ACTIVE ISSUES
# Mild alcoholic hepatitis
Patient had a long history of EtOH abuse and presented with RUQ, 
juandice, nausea, vomiting, and was found to have elevated 
transaminases (ALT 178, AST 718).  Imaging was negative for 
cholecystitis and no biliary blockage (although sludge and 
stones present).  Both US w/dopplar and HIDA scan negative. EGD 
was performed, and showed esophagitis and diffuse gastritis.  
Although patient denied recent alcohol consumption, a diagnosis 
of alcoholic hepatitis was made in the setting of strong 
clinical suspicion.  Patient received supportive treatment 
including, thiamine, folate and MVI. Steroid was not given 
considering DF of 17.  He was initially monitored on the CIWA 
protocol, not requiring benzodiapezines.  Nutrition consult was 
requested given his poor oral food intake.  His LFT improved 
daily throughout this admission.

# Thrombocytopenia
Patient presented with a platelet of 66 of unclear etiology. 
Initially subcutaneous heparin was held, then given after his 
platelets started to increase and plavix was restarted 
considering the stent history.  His platelet count improved to 
within normal range about one week after admission.

CHRONIC ISSUES
Patient has a documented history of COPD, BPH, hypothyroidism, 
urinary incontinence.  
#COPD - Patient was noted to have pursed lip breathing 
throughout this hospitalization.  Nonetheless, his lungs were 
clear to auscultation with good air movement and no wheezing, 
and maintained good oxygenation.  He was continued on his home 
medication without complications. 

#Urinary incontinence - Patient continued to have intermittent 
urinary incontinence throughout the hospitalization.  Bladder 
scan showed minimal quantities of urine < 100cc, suggesting the 
lack of retention.  Therefore, tamsulosin was discontinued.  We 
suspect that patient more likely have detrusor instability, 
causing incontinence.  He was restarted on oxybutinin.  

TRANSITIONAL ISSUES
By the time of discharge, results for anti-alpha trypsin ab, 
serum IgG, IgA are still pending.  Of note, patient has poor 
motivation for food intake, and requires repeated reminder.  
Patient maintains a full code.  He is discharged to home with 
services.  Patient is expected to see with Dr. ___ on ___ for post-discharge check up, Dr. ___ on ___ for 
liver follow-up, and Dr. ___ for GI follow-up.  The 
medication that we changed during this hospitalization include:
- started Rifaximin 550 mg twice daily
- Started to take Thiamine 100 mg daily
- Started to take multivitamin 1 tablet a day
- Decreased Trazadone dose to 50 mg daily before bed if needed 
for insomnia
- Stopped atorvastatin (lipitor) temporarily, and will need 
hepatology follow-up

Of note, patient has a hyperpigmented lesion on one of his left 
nail bed, which should be further evaluated to rule out 
melanoma.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

You were admitted to the hospital because of three days of 
nausea, vomiting, and significant belly pain. You were found to 
have esophagitis and diffuse gastritis likely related to your 
excessive alcohol use. In addition, you had significant liver 
dysfunction related to your alcohol use. You should stop 
drinking immediately and never drink again in order to prevent 
further worsening of your conditions. You were given medications 
to help treat the gastritis. Additional tests were done to 
assess your liver which showed gallstones, but no inflammation 
of your gallbladder.  Your liver markers improved significantly 
during your stay in the hospital.  You will be discharged home 
with new medications and services .

The following changes were made to your medications:
 - Please start Rifaximin 550 mg twice daily
 - Please start to take Thiamine 100 mg daily
 - Please start to take multivitamin 1 tablet a day
 - Please decrease your Trazadone dose to 50 mg daily before bed 
if needed for insomnia
 - Please STOP atorvastatin (lipitor) for now.  Your doctor may 
restart this medication if your liver function returns to 
normal.
 
We will have a medical social worker visit you at home in order 
to help get you more home services if possible.  

Your visiting nurses should draw your blood on ___ to 
obtain the labs for your follow-up appointment.

Please keep all follow-up appointments with your primary care 
doctor, liver doctors and ___ health care providers. 

Please do not drink more than 3 glasses of free water per day.

It was a pleasure taking care of you and we wish you a speedy 
recovery.
